Energy & Infrastructure · The Gridless Calculation

The 4-Percent Pivot: Gridless Finds Rural AI Compute Out-Earns Hashrate Fifteen to One

An AI container operating at just 4% utilization yields the same revenue as continuous Bitcoin mining, according to Gridless, upending the economics of mini-grids across rural Africa.

By the Observer Editorial Desk

For four years, the rural mini-grid playbook across sub-Saharan Africa has relied on a single anchor customer: the Bitcoin mining container. In communities where electricity demand grows slowly and local power revenue averages barely two to three dollars per customer each month, hashrate served as the guaranteed buyer of last resort, monetising surplus hydro and solar output from day one.

Now, data published by Gridless and reported by Federico Rivi indicates that equation is shifting rapidly. According to operational metrics from mini-grid installations, An AI container operating at just 4% utilization can generate, according to Gridless, the same revenue as a Bitcoin mining container with the same power capacity running continuously. The unit economics are stark: Each kWh sold to AI compute would be worth 15 to 25 times more than one used for hashrate.

Africa is home to nearly one-fifth of the world’s population but hosts only 0.6% of global data center capacity. While large-scale facilities require mature grid interconnects and high-capacity fiber, Gridless is deploying modular, distributed hardware: run-of-river hydro in Kenya, solar in the Democratic Republic of Congo, and prototype compute racks in Nairobi. Yet the transition is not an immediate substitution. Because AI workloads require low-latency connectivity and complex contractual pipelines that remain absent in remote valleys, Bitcoin mining retains its role as the bridge asset—the only load that converts raw megawatts into balance-sheet capital without asking whether a fiber trench has reached the village.

Source: Federico Rivi's analysis of Gridless operational filings.

Client Architecture

Amethyst 1.15.0 Rebuilds Group Messaging onto Standardized Marmot Spec

The release standardizes encrypted group channels with White Noise, introduces relay-aware search filters, and expands reading capabilities to libraries and wikis.

Amethyst rolled out version 1.15.0 on Friday evening, bringing substantial architectural refinements to Android’s most widely used Nostr client. The headline engineering effort centers on Marmot: the protocol’s group messaging implementation has been completely rebuilt against the recently adopted specification, enabling seamless bi-directional group interoperability between Amethyst and White Noise clients.

Beyond encrypted groups, the release re-engineers the application search bar so that tokenized inputs function as true multi-relay filters. Desktop users gain NIP-53 live stream discovery and participation, while the core parser now indexes publications, wiki entries, and library records. A targeted bug fix resolves Tor connection hangs that had previously stranded new installations during initial bootstrapping.

Source: Amethyst project announcement.

Dispatches & Field Reports

Security Post-Mortem

SideSwap Build Details and the 4,000 BTC Drain

Technical autopsies of the September 6 Liquid sidechain breach continued to surface uncomfortable operational revelations over the past 24 hours. Federation records show that 83 distinct inputs gathered eleven out of fifteen valid federation signatures to release 4,000 Bitcoin through standard spending paths.

According to security reconstructions by CertiK and Federico Rivi, the attackers bypassed validation by replaying accepted states. Exchange operator SideSwap acknowledged installing a private pre-release build on August 13 that processed the unauthorized transactions, while also noting that its Peg-out Authorization Key had been left active on automated forwarding with zero withdrawal caps. Blockstream has demanded the return of the remaining stolen funds while negotiations remain stalled.

Sources: Federico Rivi's breakdown and Bitcoin Magazine reporting.

Studio Reflections

The Artist's Burden: Skills, Patrons, and the Mail

Painter Flo Montoya shared a candid meditation on creative vocation on Saturday morning: Being an artist makes no sense, and I say this knowing I cannot not be an artist (I've tried).

Montoya outlined the four inescapable phases of the craft: training difficult technique, applying it toward personal meaning, finding buyers willing to pay, and finally the agony of shipping—building a custom crate only to watch couriers puncture the package. The thread struck a chord with independent makers navigating sovereign commerce.

Source: Flo Montoya's studio note.

Protocols & Payments

Xaps vs. Zaps: Monero's Quiet Test on Nostr Feeds

A subtle monetary skirmish simmered across the timeline as several active creators experimented with Monero payment targets alongside traditional Lightning addresses. After setting up a destination on the Nosmero client, JPaq reported zero zaps and zero xaps on day one, prompting a lively debate over whether privacy-preserving altcoins are finding organic demand on Nostr or merely riding speculative curiosity.

While advocates point to unshielded payment metadata as a privacy hazard on Lightning, podcast host rev.hodl pointed to the real-world grassroots divergence: dozens of in-person Bitcoin meetups happen weekly across the globe, while Monero peer gatherings remain virtually non-existent.

Sources: JPaq's experiment and rev.hodl's meetup comparison.
